editorNote: The IBM-compatible tide rises as Zenith enters the field, IBM presses its firmware claims, and PC software and accessories fill dealer pages.
morningLine: Zenith joins the compatible rush while software, mice and modems crowd the personal-computer marketplace.

lead.headline: Zenith Joins the IBM-Compatible Rush With New 16-Bit PCs
lead.dek: The electronics veteran enters the hottest race in personal computing with a 16-bit family built to speak IBM’s language.
body: Zenith Data Systems unveiled its Z-150 family on February 22, placing another substantial manufacturer in the fast-growing market for machines compatible with the IBM Personal Computer. The new 16-bit line is aimed at buyers who want access to the expanding IBM software world without buying an IBM-badged machine.

Compatibility has become the industry’s most valuable promise. Businesses are accumulating programs, files and training around the PC standard, and every new entrant must convince customers that familiar software and peripherals will travel safely to its hardware. Zenith brings an established dealer and institutional presence to that contest.

The arrival also sharpens a difficult question: how closely may a rival follow IBM’s design? The week’s settlement between IBM and Eagle Computer over firmware copyright shows that software hidden inside the box can matter as much as the chips and disk drives advertised outside it.

For buyers, the result is a broader field and more pressure on prices. For manufacturers, it is a race to offer compatibility while retaining enough engineering independence to stay outside IBM’s legal sights.

stories.headline: IBM and Eagle Settle Firmware Copyright Fight
body: IBM and Eagle Computer settled their dispute over copyrighted firmware this week, adding a legal boundary marker to the compatible-computer boom. IBM has argued that copying the code that starts and controls a PC infringes its copyright even when a rival builds otherwise independent hardware.

The settlement warns clone makers that compatibility cannot simply mean reproducing IBM’s internal instructions. Manufacturers increasingly need independently written firmware—a clean route to the same behavior—if they want to sell access to PC software without inviting a courtroom fight.

stories.headline: Software Industry Comes Into Its Own
body: The personal-computer software trade is emerging as an industry in its own right, with applications, utilities and specialist publishers multiplying around popular machines. Dealer pages now present software as a shelf of competing products rather than an afterthought bundled with hardware.

Microsoft is pushing Word alongside its mouse, while database managers promise links to spreadsheets and word processors and small utilities such as Norton’s win space in the same crowded market. The value of a computer increasingly rests on what buyers can make it do after the box reaches the desk.

stories.headline: PC Magazine Pits Apple Experience Against IBM Momentum
body: PC Magazine’s February issue captures a market divided between Apple’s carefully designed user experience and the IBM PC’s gathering commercial momentum. Buyers are weighing graphical ease and integration against the immense tide of compatible hardware and software.

That contrast is shaping the next phase of personal computing. Apple asks users to adopt a distinct way of working; the IBM camp offers a widening bazaar of interchangeable pieces, dealer discounts and familiar business programs.

briefs.headline: Van Halen's synth-powered 'Jump' takes the pop summit
briefs.text: The record moved to No. 1 for the chart dated February 25, while '99 Luftballons,' 'Thriller,' and 'Footloose' were climbing rapidly.

briefs.text: A monitor, RAM board, modem, storage, and software could add hundreds or thousands of dollars beyond the base computer, as contemporary PC Magazine dealer pages show.

worldAnchor.headline: U.S. Marines Begin Leaving Beirut
worldAnchor.summary: UPI reported February 21 that Marines were leaving Lebanon after 17 months, with the government they had supported badly weakened; the withdrawal and Reagan's defense of the deployment dominated the week's foreign-policy news.
